title: Webb v. McGowin
lead: A mill worker permanently injures himself while saving another man from a falling block. The rescued man promises lifetime installments and pays for years; after his death, the worker sues the estate for unpaid installments.

actors.name: Joe Webb
actors.role: Lumber-company employee and injured rescuer seeking promised support.

actors.name: J. Greeley McGowin
actors.role: Man saved by Webb who later promised payment.

actors.name: McGowin’s executors
actors.role: Estate representatives defending against the installment claim.

proceedings: The trial court sustained demurrers; Webb took a nonsuit and appealed.
The Alabama Court of Appeals reversed and remanded, later denying rehearing.
The Alabama Supreme Court denied certiorari in a separate opinion approving the material-benefit principle it discussed.
limits: This transforms the canonical historical brief without a fresh audit or current-law certification. Facts were pleaded and tested on demurrer, not found after trial. The reported inability to perform physical or mental labor is preserved as alleged disability, not an independent cognitive diagnosis. The Supreme Court certiorari opinion is a distinct later judicial stage.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Webb diverts a heavy block at the cost of his own safety
sections.cue: Was there a bargain before the rescue?
paragraphs: On August 3, 1925, Joe Webb was clearing an upper floor for the W. T. Smith Lumber Company. The ordinary method was to drop waste to the ground. Preparing to drop a pine block weighing about seventy-five pounds, he saw J. Greeley McGowin directly in its expected path. The complaint alleged that release probably would kill or seriously injure McGowin.

Webb could safely let go. Instead, he retained the block and fell with it, changing its path and protecting McGowin from injury. Webb badly injured his right leg, heel, and arm and was permanently disabled, described in the pleadings as unable to perform physical or mental labor. No prior compensation agreement or actual request by McGowin was alleged.

sections.title: McGowin promises support and performs for more than eight years
sections.cue: Why did the claimed obligation extend beyond his death?
paragraphs: On September 1, 1925, McGowin allegedly promised Webb fifteen dollars every two weeks for the rest of Webb’s life, recognizing both the lifesaving service and the injuries. Payments continued more than eight years until McGowin died January 1, 1934, and continued through January 27 before stopping.

Webb sued McGowin’s executors in assumpsit, the historical action used to enforce this undertaking, for installments accruing after January 27 through commencement of suit. The promise’s endpoint was Webb’s life, not McGowin’s. After amendment, the trial court sustained demurrers asserting no cause of action, no consideration or prior agreement, and the Statute of Frauds. Webb took a nonsuit because of that ruling and appealed.

sections.title: Bricken treats preserving life as a material benefit
sections.cue: Why was this more than gratitude alone?
paragraphs: Presiding Judge Bricken’s Court of Appeals opinion held the allegations sufficient. A moral obligation linked to an actual material benefit could support a later express promise even without an original legal payment duty. Saving a person’s life or body from serious harm was such a benefit.

The court rejected treating saved property as valuable but its saved owner as merely sentimental. Emergency antidote treatment, care of an escaped animal, preservation of property, medical compensation, injury damages, and life or accident insurance all illustrated recognition of bodily and material interests. The point was not a market price for McGowin’s life or an award of that value, but a substantial benefit capable of supporting his specified undertaking.

The rescue also imposed severe loss on Webb, which McGowin’s promise expressly recognized. Years of payment and acceptance supported a compensatory arrangement rather than detached gifts. The court’s statement that the services were not gratuitous looked backward from that later conduct; it did not establish that Webb expected reward while falling.

sections.title: Ratification supplies a legal explanation despite the sequence
sections.cue: What boundaries did the court retain?
paragraphs: Bricken acknowledged decisions enforcing later promises only when an earlier legal or equitable duty had become unenforceable, but recognized a qualification for material benefits conferred directly on the promisor. The later express undertaking ratified the completed service and carried a presumption of prior request. That was doctrinal reasoning, not a finding that McGowin called to Webb or negotiated before the rescue.

The court distinguished promises by later purchasers for improvements made while land still belonged to the United States: those promisors were not the relevant owners when the services were rendered. McGowin himself received Webb’s protection. Thus the holding did not make everyone’s subsequent gratitude sufficient.

In a separate brief paragraph, the court rejected the Statute of Frauds objection without extended explanation. Judge Samford concurred, acknowledging uncertainty under strict common-law formulations but emphasizing that doubtful law should not be divorced from justice. He supplied neither a separate damages measure nor a rule dispensing with these facts.

sources.pinpoint: 27 Ala. App. 86, numbered discussions and Samford concurrence

sections.title: The appellate reversal survives later Supreme Court review
sections.cue: What did each court’s judgment accomplish?
paragraphs: On November 12, 1935, the Court of Appeals reversed the demurrer ruling and remanded for further proceedings. It did not enter a quantified award for all future installments. The report records rehearing denied February 18, 1936, without a separate reproduced merits opinion.

On May 14, 1936, Justice Foster’s Alabama Supreme Court opinion denied certiorari. He cautioned that denial ordinarily did not endorse every lower-court principle, but expressly agreed here that an actual material and substantial personal benefit could support an executed payment or executory promise, strengthened by the rescuer’s injury. Earlier public-payment decisions did not justify rewards for mere courtesy or refined moral sentiment. Chief Justice Anderson and Justices Gardner and Bouldin joined that later opinion.

The rescue preceded the promise, so this was neither an ordinary negotiated exchange nor action taken in reliance on promised payments. Compared with Mills, the later promisor personally received the benefit. Harrington, however, also involved a direct lifesaving benefit and later promise yet applied contrary consideration reasoning, so direct benefit alone did not reconcile every rescue precedent.

sources.pinpoint: 27 Ala. App. 82, 86; 232 Ala. 374–375; canonical brief’s comparative discussion
